planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the orange-flowered form of fragrant tea olive is a Gulf South favorite for its intensely apricot-scented fall bloom.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it near a window, porch, or path where its powerful fragrance can be enjoyed. Orange Tea Olive bears small, warm orange flowers, more strongly colored than the creamy-white blooms of the common fragrant tea olive, releasing an intense, sweet, apricot-like scent that carries a considerable distance on the air, most heavily in fall with lighter, scattered flushes through the rest of the year in mild climates. Its dense, glossy, evergreen foliage makes it useful as a large screening shrub, informal hedge, or small specimen tree over time, tolerating shearing well if a more formal shape is wanted. It is slower-growing and generally less cold-hardy than the plain white-flowered species, so it performs best in the milder parts of the Gulf South, and established plants need only routine watering during dry spells and an occasional shaping after the heaviest bloom flush.

common_name: Icee Blue Podocarpus (Compact Blue-Gray Foliage Yew Pine)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Icee Blue is a compact, slow-growing podocarpus selected for striking blue-gray needle-like foliage rather than the plain green of the species.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants tolerate considerable drought and are generally untroubled by pests or disease. Icee Blue produces dense, upright, needle-like foliage in a cool, silvery blue-gray that stands out sharply from the deep green of most broadleaf evergreens, giving it strong textural and color value as a specimen, foundation planting, or informal screen. Its compact, slow-growing habit needs little pruning to maintain a neat shape, unlike faster-growing podocarpus selections that require regular shearing to control size. It tolerates coastal conditions and urban pollution well and is generally free of significant pest or disease problems, needing only an occasional light shaping if a more formal form is desired and routine watering during establishment.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Jade Tiara is a variegated form of the widely planted plain-green Ternstroemia (cleyera), brightening shaded foundation beds and borders.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; some direct sun helps develop the pink and bronze tones in new growth, while deeper shade shifts the plant toward a quieter cream-and-green look. Jade Tiara bears glossy, leathery leaves edged in a bright creamy-white margin, with new growth flushing pink to bronze before settling into the mature variegated pattern, a brighter option than the solid dark green of the straight Ternstroemia species commonly used as a Southern foundation and hedge shrub. Its dense, upright habit works well as a specimen, informal screen, or accent among darker-leaved evergreens where the variegation can stand out. It tolerates both sun and considerable shade and needs only an occasional shaping cut to maintain a neat form, along with routine watering during establishment and dry spells.

common_name: Nana Rotundifolia Aucuba (Compact Round-Leaved Heavy-Berrying Gold Dust Plant)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Nana Rotundifolia is a compact, female, plain-green aucuba selection that sets heavy crops of red berries when a male aucuba is planted nearby for pollination.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; aucuba is one of the most reliable shrubs for deep, dry shade under trees where few other broadleaf evergreens perform well. Nana Rotundifolia forms a dense, rounded, compact mound of glossy, deep green, rounded leaves, more solid green than the gold-speckled forms sold as Gold Dust Plant, and as a female selection it produces heavy clusters of bright red berries in fall and winter when a male aucuba cultivar is planted nearby to provide pollen. Its naturally tidy, slow-growing habit needs little pruning to maintain shape, making it useful for foundation plantings, mass plantings, or a low, dark green backdrop for shade perennials. It tolerates heavy shade, dry soil once established, and general neglect better than most broadleaf evergreens, needing only routine watering during establishment and occasional shaping if desired.
